keyTerms.definition: Assigns numbers in [0,1] to discrete outcomes; sums to 1.
Assigns non-negative values per unit of x to a continuum; integrates to 1.

recall.question: State the normalization rule for probability and for density.
recall.answer: Probability sums to 1 over discrete outcomes. Density integrates to 1 over the continuum.

keyTerms.definition: The set {x : p(x) > 0}.
The full set of possible outcomes; support can be smaller.

recall.question: Give the support of the toy law and of N(0,1).
recall.answer: Toy: {R, G, B}. N(0,1): the whole real line.

keyTerms.definition: Z = 6+4+2 = 12: the normalizer of the scores.
Scores divided by Z: (0.5, 0.333, 0.167).

recall.question: Compute Z and the law for scores (6,4,2).
recall.answer: Z = 12. Law = (0.5, 0.333, 0.167). Red flag: forgetting to divide.

keyTerms.definition: p(color|L): the column renormalized by its own sum.
The column sum 6; dividing by the row sum is the red flag.

recall.question: Compute p(color|L) for column L = (2,3,1).
recall.answer: (2,3,1)/6 = (0.333, 0.5, 0.167). Divide by the column sum, not the row sum.

keyTerms.definition: p(data | parameters) with data fixed.
12 ln(1/3) = -13.183 nats under the uniform law.

recall.question: What is the log-likelihood of the twelve draws under the uniform law?

keyTerms.definition: Puts mass 1/n on each observed sample.
An outcome never observed; the empirical law gives it mass 0.

recall.question: What mass does the empirical distribution put on an unseen outcome?
recall.answer: 0. It is a perfect memory of the data and does not generalize.

keyTerms.definition: H(p) = -sum p log p: expected surprise in nats.
R -> 0, G -> 10, B -> 11: the code designed on this rung.
Gives H <= ln K; shows uniform maximizes entropy.

recall.question: What is the expected code length on the L1 rung, and how does it compare to entropy?
recall.answer: 1.5 bits, above the toy law's H = 1.459 bits. A code cannot beat entropy.

recall.question: Why does uniform maximize entropy?
recall.answer: -log is convex and symmetry forces the maximum at equality. Jensen gives H <= ln K.

keyTerms.definition: Maximum a posteriori: a Dirichlet prior adds one fake count per outcome.
E[theta_hat] - theta: systematic error.
E[(theta_hat - E)^2]: wobble across datasets.

recall.question: What does the Dirichlet prior with alpha=2 do to the n=1 MLE (1,0,0)?
recall.answer: It adds one fake count per outcome: posterior counts (2,1,1) over 4, giving (0.5, 0.25, 0.25).

recall.question: When should you use MLE over MAP?
recall.answer: When n is large enough that prior washout is complete. Rule of thumb: n >> K * alpha.

keyTerms.definition: E[-log(q/p)] >= -log E[q/p]: the convex flip that proves KL >= 0.
KL = 0 exactly when q/p is constant a.s., i.e. p = q.

recall.question: Prove KL(p||q) >= 0 and state the equality condition.
recall.answer: KL = E_p[-log(q/p)]. -log is convex, so Jensen gives E[-log(q/p)] >= -log 1 = 0. Equality exactly when p = q.

keyTerms.definition: lambda: enforces the sum-to-1 constraint in the MLE derivation.
theta_i = c_i / n: counts over n.

recall.question: Derive the categorical MLE.
recall.answer: Maximize sum c_i log theta_i + lambda(1 - sum theta_i). The derivative gives theta_i = c_i/lambda; the constraint gives lambda = n, so theta_i = c_i/n.

keyTerms.definition: The buggy call searched edges including 0.0, shifting every bin up by one.
120000 draws, chi-square against p_hat, p > 0.01.

recall.question: What is the sampler bug and the fix?
recall.answer: searchsorted over edges including 0.0 maps u in [0,0.5) to index 1 and u near 1 out of range. Fix: searchsorted(edges[1:], u).

keyTerms.definition: The MLE gives the unseen fourth color mass 0, breaking KL in one direction.
The remedy for zero mass on unseen outcomes.

recall.question: What breaks when the bag gains a fourth unseen color?
recall.answer: The MLE is (0.5, 0.333, 0.167, 0) and claims the fourth color is impossible. KL(uniform4||p_hat) is infinite. Remedy: smoothing.

keyTerms.definition: Keep c and total n; update c[x] += 1, n += 1 per draw.
Memory cost of the running-counts scheme; O(1) per draw.

recall.question: How do you maintain the empirical law online?
recall.answer: Keep running counts c and total n. On new draw x: c[x] += 1, n += 1, p_emp = c/n on demand. O(K) memory, O(1) per draw.

keyTerms.definition: Scores the model on test points; the settling experiment's decision metric.
Requires checking model support on test points.

recall.question: Give two counterexamples to 'higher training likelihood means a better generative model'.
recall.answer: One: the empirical distribution gets the best training likelihood and memorizes. Two: a model with support inside the data support can win on covered training points while giving zero mass to real held-out points.
